title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
notes:
Task and constraints: Choose one buy day and a later sell day to maximize profit. If no profitable transaction exists, return zero.
Idea: Scan prices once, tracking the lowest price seen so far and the best difference between the current price and that minimum.
Technique and why it applies: For any sell day, the best buy day before it is the minimum earlier price, so one running minimum covers every possible transaction ending there.
Invariant: Before processing a price, the minimum is the lowest price among earlier days and best is the best profit achievable so far.
Edge cases: A decreasing sequence yields zero profit. At least one price is supplied.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A single pass updates the minimum price and maximum profit.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize total profit when any number of buy/sell transactions is allowed, but only one share can be held at a time.
Idea: Add every positive difference between consecutive prices to the total profit.
Technique and why it applies: A rising run's full gain equals the sum of its daily increases, and separating positive increases captures every profitable segment without overlapping holdings.
Invariant: The accumulated total equals the sum of all positive adjacent price changes processed so far.
Edge cases: Flat or decreasing adjacent prices contribute zero. A monotonically rising sequence yields last price minus first price.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each adjacent price pair contributes at most one difference.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
approach_name: Track two buys and two sells
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize stock-trading profit with at most two complete transactions and no simultaneous holdings.
Idea: Maintain the best balance after first buy, first sell, second buy, and second sell. Update these states in order for every price.
Technique and why it applies: Each state represents the best result after a particular transaction action, and a later action can build on the best earlier state.
Invariant: After processing each price, each state is the best achievable value for its corresponding transaction stage using prices seen so far.
Edge cases: Zero or one transaction may be optimal. Negative intermediate buy states represent cost, not actual negative profit.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Four scalar states summarize all relevant transaction histories.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
approach_name: Return one-sided gain and update global path
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum sum of any non-empty path in a binary tree. A path may start and end at any nodes but cannot branch or revisit a node.
Idea: For each node, compute the maximum gain from that node downward through at most one child. Update a global best with node value plus positive gains from both children.
Technique and why it applies: A path passing through a node can combine its left and right downward gains, while a parent can extend only one side.
Invariant: The recursive gain is the best downward path starting at the node; the global best records any path whose highest point has been processed.
Edge cases: All values may be negative, so initialize the global best to negative infinity. Ignore negative child gains.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once and recursion follows the tree height.

title: Valid Palindrome
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a string is a palindrome after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and letter case.
Idea: Move pointers inward from both ends, skipping characters that are not alphanumeric. Compare the remaining characters case-insensitively and stop on a mismatch.
Technique and why it applies: A palindrome is symmetric, so only paired characters from the two ends need comparison; filtering can happen during the scan.
Invariant: All character pairs outside the active interval have matched after normalization.
Edge cases: An empty or all-punctuation string is a palindrome. Unicode alphanumeric classification follows the language's standard character helpers.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each pointer moves inward and no filtered copy is built.

title: Word Ladder II
approach_name: BFS parent graph then reconstruct shortest paths
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all shortest sequences transforming beginWord to endWord by changing one character at a time, with every intermediate word in the dictionary.
Idea: BFS by levels to record every parent that reaches a word at its shortest distance. Once the end word is found at a level, stop after processing that entire level; then backtrack through the parent graph to enumerate paths.
Technique and why it applies: BFS guarantees shortest distances, while retaining all same-level parents preserves every shortest sequence.
Invariant: Each parent edge points from a word at one distance to a word at the next distance along a shortest path.
Edge cases: If endWord is absent, return no paths. Do not remove a discovered word before all parents from the same BFS level have been recorded.
Complexity: Time is output-sensitive and can be exponential in the number of shortest paths. Space stores the parent graph and paths.
space_complexity: O(words × word length + parent graph + output)
complexity_reason: BFS records shortest-level parent edges, and DFS enumerates every shortest path.

title: Word Ladder
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of words in the shortest transformation from beginWord to endWord, changing one character at a time and using dictionary words for intermediate results.
Idea: BFS from beginWord. Generate each one-letter mutation, enqueue unseen dictionary words, and return the current distance when endWord is reached.
Technique and why it applies: Each transformation has equal cost, so BFS explores words in increasing path length and finds the shortest sequence first.
Invariant: A word is marked visited when enqueued, preventing it from entering the queue more than once.
Edge cases: If endWord is not in the dictionary, return zero. If beginWord equals endWord, the sequence length is one.
Complexity: Time is O(N·L·26·L) with string construction in this implementation; space is O(N·L), where N is dictionary size and L word length.
complexity_reason: Each dictionary word is visited once and each position tries alphabet replacements.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integer values in an unsorted array, in expected linear time.
Idea: Put values in a set. For each value that has no predecessor value-1, walk forward while consecutive values exist and record the run length.
Technique and why it applies: Starting only at sequence beginnings prevents repeatedly scanning the same run from every interior value.
Invariant: Every run is measured from its smallest value, where no predecessor is present.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. Duplicate values do not extend a run because the set stores each value once.
Complexity: Time is O(n) expected because each value participates in at most one forward run. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each unique value is inserted once; forward scans begin only at sequence starts.

title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Each root-to-leaf path represents a decimal number formed by concatenating node digits. Return the sum of all represented numbers.
Idea: During DFS, update the prefix as prefix*10 + node.val. At each leaf, return that complete number; otherwise sum the results from both children.
Technique and why it applies: Appending a decimal digit shifts the current number left by one decimal place and adds the new digit.
Invariant: The prefix argument is exactly the number represented by the path from root to the current node.
Edge cases: An empty tree contributes zero. Leaf checks must require both children to be absent.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once and recursion carries the current path number.

title: Surrounded Regions
notes:
Task and constraints: Capture every O region that is not connected to the board boundary by flipping it to X. Boundary-connected O cells must remain O.
Idea: Start from boundary O cells and flood-fill them with a temporary marker. After all boundary-connected regions are marked, flip remaining O cells to X and restore the markers to O.
Technique and why it applies: Only regions connected to a boundary can escape capture, so identifying those safe cells is sufficient.
Invariant: Every temporarily marked cell is reachable from the boundary through O cells.
Edge cases: Boards with fewer than three rows or columns have no fully enclosed interior region. Avoid revisiting already marked cells.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(mn) for the queue in this BFS implementation.
complexity_reason: Each cell is marked and queued at most once.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all partitions of a string where every segment is a palindrome.
Idea: Starting at an index, try each ending position. If the substring is a palindrome, append it to the path and recurse from the next index; copy the path when the string is fully consumed.
Technique and why it applies: Each valid partition has a first palindrome prefix followed by another valid partition of the remaining suffix.
Invariant: Every segment in the path is palindromic, and the path covers exactly the prefix before the current index.
Edge cases: A one-character string has one partition. An empty string conventionally yields one empty partition.
Complexity: The number of partitions can be exponential; substring checks add up to O(n·2^n) worst-case time. Auxiliary space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: Each partition branch is explored and substring palindrome checks scan up to n characters.

title: Palindrome Partitioning II
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum number of cuts needed to split a string into palindromic substrings.
Idea: Build a palindrome table pal[start][end]. For each end position, initialize its cut count to the worst case of one character per piece, then improve it for every palindromic suffix using zero cuts when it starts at zero or cuts[start-1]+1 otherwise.
Technique and why it applies: Once palindrome intervals are known, the best partition ending at each position depends on the best partition before its final palindrome.
Invariant: cuts[i] is the minimum cuts for the prefix ending at i, and pal marks exactly the palindromic intervals already recognized.
Edge cases: A one-character string requires zero cuts. An all-palindrome string also needs zero cuts.
Complexity: Time and space are O(n^2) for the table and transitions.
complexity_reason: Each substring is considered once and each end position checks its possible starts.

title: Clone Graph
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a deep copy of a connected undirected graph. Each cloned node must be a new object with the same value and neighbor relationships.
Idea: Use a map from original nodes to their clones. When a node is first seen, create its clone and traverse its neighbors; append each neighbor's clone to the clone's neighbor list.
Technique and why it applies: Graphs may contain cycles and shared neighbors, so the map prevents infinite recursion and preserves node identity across edges.
Invariant: Every visited original node has exactly one clone in the map, and its processed neighbor links mirror the original links.
Edge cases: A null input returns null. The graph may contain cycles and self-loops.
Complexity: Time and space are O(V+E) for nodes and edges.
space_complexity: O(V) for the clone map and traversal stack
complexity_reason: Each node is cloned once and each edge is copied once.

title: Gas Station
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the unique station index from which a car can complete a circular route, given gas at each station and the cost to reach the next station; return -1 if impossible.
Idea: Track total net gas and the current tank. If the tank becomes negative at station i, no start within the current candidate segment can reach beyond i, so choose i+1 as the next candidate and reset the tank.
Technique and why it applies: If total gas covers total cost, the greedy reset identifies a feasible start; otherwise no circuit can exist.
Invariant: The candidate start has non-negative running tank for every station since that candidate.
Edge cases: If total gas is less than total cost, return -1. The valid starting index is unique under the problem guarantee.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A single pass tracks total surplus, current tank, and candidate start.

title: Candy
notes:
Task and constraints: Give each child at least one candy, and give a child with a higher rating more candies than each lower-rated immediate neighbor. Minimize the total candies.
Idea: Initialize every child with one candy. Scan left-to-right to satisfy rising ratings, then right-to-left to satisfy falling ratings by taking the maximum of the current allocation and right-neighbor allocation plus one.
Technique and why it applies: Each pass enforces one directional neighbor constraint; taking the maximum combines both requirements without violating the first pass.
Invariant: After the first pass, every rising adjacent pair is valid; after the second, every falling pair is also valid.
Edge cases: Equal ratings impose no extra candy requirement. Strictly increasing and decreasing sequences need a ramp of allocations.
Complexity: Time and space are O(n).
complexity_reason: Two directional passes maintain one allocation per child.

title: Single Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Every value in the array appears twice except one value that appears once. Find that value in linear time and constant extra space.
Idea: XOR all elements. Equal pairs cancel because x XOR x is zero, and XOR with zero leaves the other operand unchanged.
Technique and why it applies: XOR is associative and commutative, so the order of the values does not matter and all paired values disappear.
Invariant: The running XOR equals the XOR of all values processed so far.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns that element. Negative integers work with the language's fixed-width or arbitrary-precision bitwise XOR semantics for this cancellation property.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each number is XORed into one accumulator.

title: Single Number II
approach_name: Track bits appearing once and twice
notes:
Task and constraints: Every value appears three times except one value that appears once. Find the unique value in linear time and constant extra space.
Idea: Maintain bit masks ones and twos. For each number, toggle its bits in ones, then remove from ones bits already represented in twos; update twos similarly while excluding the new ones mask.
Technique and why it applies: Each bit's state cycles through counts modulo three, so bits contributed by triplicated values cancel from the final ones mask.
Invariant: ones contains bits seen once modulo three and twos contains bits seen twice modulo three.
Edge cases: Negative values are supported by fixed-width bit operations in Java and Python's bitwise identities. The final ones mask is the unique value.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Two bit masks summarize the count state for all 32 bit positions.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
notes:
Task and constraints: Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes have next and random pointers. Random may point to any node in the list or null.
Idea: First create a clone for every node reachable through next, storing original-to-copy mappings. In a second pass, assign each clone's next and random pointers to the mapped clones of the corresponding original targets.
Technique and why it applies: A map preserves identity relationships and handles random pointers that point forward, backward, or to the same node.
Invariant: Every original list node has exactly one clone before pointer relationships are connected.
Edge cases: A null head returns null. Random pointers may be null or self-referential.
Complexity: Time and space are O(n).
complexity_reason: The map stores one clone per original node and supports constant-expected-time pointer lookup.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def copyRandomList(self, head: Optional[Node]) -> Optional[Node]:
        if not head:return None
        clones={};node=head
        while node:clones[node]=Node(node.val);node=node.next
        node=head
        while node:
            clones[node].next=clones.get(node.next)
            clones[node].random=clones.get(node.random)
            node=node.next
        return clones[head]

title: Word Break
approach_name: Check dictionary words ending at each prefix
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a string can be segmented into dictionary words, reusing dictionary entries as often as needed.
Idea: Let dp[i] indicate whether the prefix s[:i] can be segmented. For each end position, test earlier split points; if dp[start] is true and s[start:end] is in the dictionary, mark dp[end] true.
Technique and why it applies: Any valid segmentation ends with a dictionary word preceded by a valid segmentation of the earlier prefix.
Invariant: dp[i] is true exactly when the first i characters can be split into dictionary words.
Edge cases: The empty prefix is segmentable, so dp[0] is true. A dictionary word may be used multiple times.
Complexity: O(n^2) substring checks expected, with additional substring construction overhead. Space is O(n) plus the dictionary.
time_complexity: O(n^2) expected membership checks, plus substring costs
complexity_reason: Each prefix tests possible final word boundaries until one valid split is found.

title: Word Break
approach_name: Check dictionary words ending at each prefix
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a string can be segmented into dictionary words, reusing dictionary entries as often as needed.
Idea: Let dp[i] indicate whether the prefix s[:i] can be segmented. For each end position, test earlier split points; if dp[start] is true and s[start:end] is in the dictionary, mark dp[end] true.
Technique and why it applies: Any valid segmentation ends with a dictionary word preceded by a valid segmentation of the earlier prefix.
Invariant: dp[i] is true exactly when the first i characters can be split into dictionary words.
Edge cases: The empty prefix is segmentable, so dp[0] is true. A dictionary word may be used multiple times.
Complexity: O(n^2) substring checks expected, with additional substring construction overhead. Space is O(n) plus the dictionary.
time_complexity: O(n^2) expected membership checks, plus substring costs
complexity_reason: Each prefix tests possible final word boundaries until one valid split is found.

title: Word Break II
approach_name: Memoize sentence suffixes by start index
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every sentence formed by inserting spaces so that each resulting word belongs to the dictionary.
Idea: Memoize all valid sentences that can be formed from each starting index. Try every dictionary word matching the current prefix, then combine it with sentences from the remaining suffix.
Technique and why it applies: The suffix after a chosen word is independent of the earlier choices, so caching its sentence list avoids recomputing the same suffix repeatedly.
Invariant: The memoized list for index i contains exactly all valid sentences for s[i:].
Edge cases: If no word matches a suffix, its memoized result is empty. The output may be exponential, so output size dominates in worst cases.
Complexity: Time and space are output-sensitive and can be exponential in string length.
complexity_reason: Each start index is expanded once, but each valid sentence must still be materialized.
